techniques.name: Partial Dependence Plots
techniques.description: Partial Dependence Plots show how changing one or two features affects a model's predictions on average. The technique works by varying the selected feature(s) across their full range whilst keeping all other features fixed at their original values, then averaging the predictions. This creates a clear visualisation of whether increasing or decreasing a feature tends to increase or decrease predictions, and reveals patterns like linear trends, plateaus, or threshold effects that help explain model behaviour.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing how house prices change with property size in a real estate prediction model, revealing whether the relationship is linear or if there are diminishing returns for very large properties.
Examining how customer age affects predicted loan default probability in a credit scoring model, showing whether risk increases steadily with age or has specific age ranges with higher risk.
Visualising how temperature affects crop yield predictions in agricultural models, identifying optimal temperature ranges and potential threshold effects.

limitations.description: Assumes the plotted features are independent of the others. When they are correlated, the averaging pairs values that never occur together, so the curve partly reflects how the model behaves in regions with no data.

Shows only the average effect. If a feature acts in opposite directions for different groups of instances, the effects cancel and the curve can look flat, so interactions with other features stay hidden.
Limited to one or two features at a time, because higher-dimensional plots cannot be read. Effects that depend on three or more features together cannot be shown.
The basic method needs a pass over the whole dataset for every grid value, so cost grows with dataset size, the number of grid points and the time the model takes to predict.

resources.title: Greedy function approximation: A gradient boosting machine.
resources.abstract: Function estimation/approximation is viewed from the perspective of numerical optimization in function space, rather than parameter space. A connection is made between stagewise additive expansions and steepest-descent minimization. A general gradient descent “boosting” paradigm is developed for additive expansions based on any fitting criterion.Specific algorithms are presented for least-squares, least absolute deviation, and Huber-M loss functions for regression, and multiclass logistic likelihood for classification. Special enhancements are derived for the particular case where the individual additive components are regression trees, and tools for interpreting such “TreeBoost” models are presented. Gradient boosting of regression trees produces competitive, highly robust, interpretable procedures for both regression and classification, especially appropriate for mining less than clean data. Connections between this approach and the boosting methods of Freund and Shapire and Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani are discussed.

resources.title: Using machine learning to examine freight network spatial vulnerabilities to disasters: A new take on partial dependence plots
resources.abstract: Analyzing transportation network vulnerabilities to disruptions is crucial for society to maintain commodity flows across the globe. However, most vulnerability analyses focus on impacts that arise from the deterioration of single network components, which can overlook spatial correlations between multiple components that manifest during area-spanning disruptions, such as those stemming from natural hazards. Here, we demonstrate an intuitive, simulation-based approach for inferring spatial vulnerabilities to area-spanning disruptions. In particular, we show how partial dependence plots derived from gradient boosting machines trained on the results of a routing simulation can be used to depict the average effect a disruption’s location has on impacts while controlling for other input variables and spatial dependencies embedded in the network. Although we demonstrate our approach for Middle Tennessee’s intermodal road and rail freight transportation network, our framework can easily be applied to other networks.

resources.title: Uncovering nonlinear patterns in time-sensitive prehospital breathing emergencies: an exploratory machine learning study
resources.abstract: Background Timely prehospital care is crucial for patients presenting with high-risk time-sensitive (HRTS) conditions. However, the interplay between response time and demographic factors in patients with breathing problems remains insufficiently understood. In this exploratory study, we applied machine learning (ML) to examine how emergency medical response time, age, and sex jointly influence the probability of encountering HRTS conditions. Methods A retrospective observational analysis was conducted on 132,395 prehospital missions in Stockholm (2017–2022). Multiple ML models, random forest, gradient boosting, neural networks, and logistic regression were trained to probe potential nonlinear patterns and interactions, not with the primary goal of predictive accuracy. Model performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC) measures. However, partial dependence (PD) and individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots were the principal tools illustrating how response time, age, and sex shape HRTS likelihood. Results PD and ICE plots revealed that older age (> 60 years) was consistently associated with a higher probability of HRTS. Moreover, patients over 60 years displayed a complex, rising risk at prolonged response times exceeding two hours. Gradient boosting offered the best (though modest) classification metrics, with an AUC of 0.66 and an F1-score of 0.55. We emphasize that these metrics, while necessary for completeness, were secondary to our aim of characterizing nonlinear relationships. Conclusions Our findings underscore the exploratory value of ML in identifying subtle relationships and interactions among response time, age, and sex for time-sensitive breathing emergencies. These results highlight opportunities to refine dispatch protocols, develop age- and sex-focused screening questions, and revisit lower-priority calls after extended wait times. Future work should incorporate richer data and refine these insights for potential predictive use. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

techniques.name: Individual Conditional Expectation Plots
techniques.description: Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) plots display the predicted output for individual instances as a function of a feature, with all other features held fixed for each instance. Each line on an ICE plot represents one instance's prediction trajectory as the feature of interest changes, revealing whether different instances are affected differently by that feature. This complements Partial Dependence Plots by showing heterogeneous effects across individual instances rather than just the average trend.

example_use_cases.description: A valuation team checks a house-price model before using it for automated estimates. ICE lines for property age show most homes losing value as they age, but a group of pre-1900 homes gaining value. The team asks whether the model has learned a real heritage premium or is reacting to a handful of unusual sales.

A hospital data science team reviews a diabetes risk model before clinicians use it. ICE lines of predicted risk against BMI rise steadily for most patients but stay flat for a small group. The team colours the lines by recorded characteristics, such as age band, to see what the flat group shares, then asks a clinician whether a flat response is plausible.

A credit risk validation team marks each applicant's actual income on that applicant's ICE line for a loan pricing model. For some applicant profiles the line changes steeply at incomes where no similar applicants appear in the training data. The team treats that part of the line as extrapolation and restricts the model's use to the supported range.

limitations.description: With hundreds or thousands of cases the lines overlap into a dense band that hides individual behaviour. Plotting a sample of lines, shifting them to start at the same point, or colouring them by a second feature is usually needed before the plot can be read.

Each line changes one feature while holding the case's other features fixed. Where features are correlated, parts of a line describe combinations that never occur in the data, so the model is extrapolating there. Marking each case's actual feature value on its line shows which part of the line the data supports.

Lines that are not parallel show that the feature's effect depends on other features, but not which ones. Finding out means colouring the lines by candidate features one at a time, so the search is by trial and error.

Judging whether lines differ by more than chance is done by eye, and a model can produce uneven lines from noise alone. The authors' formal check hides the real plot among plots made from additive fits, which needs the model to be refitted many times.

In its basic form the plot needs a model prediction for every case at every observed value of the feature, so the number of predictions grows with the square of the dataset size. Large datasets or slow models call for sampling.

resources.title: Peeking Inside the Black Box: Visualizing Statistical Learning with Plots of Individual Conditional Expectation
resources.abstract: This article presents Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) plots, a tool for visualizing the model estimated by any supervised learning algorithm. Classical partial dependence plots (PDPs) help visualize the average partial relationship between the predicted response and one or more features. In the presence of substantial interaction effects, the partial response relationship can be heterogeneous. Thus, an average curve, such as the PDP, can obfuscate the complexity of the modeled relationship. Accordingly, ICE plots refine the partial dependence plot by graphing the functional relationship between the predicted response and the feature for individual observations. Specifically, ICE plots highlight the variation in the fitted values across the range of a covariate, suggesting where and to what extent heterogeneities might exist. In addition to providing a plotting suite for exploratory analysis, we include a visual test for additive structure in the data generating model. Through simulated examples and real data sets, we demonstrate how ICE plots can shed light on estimated models in ways PDPs cannot. Procedures outlined are available in the R package ICEbox.

resources.title: Identification of Trends in Dam Monitoring Data Series Based on Machine Learning and Individual Conditional Expectation Curves
resources.abstract: Dams are complex systems that involve both the structure itself and its foundation. Rheological phenomena, expansive reactions, or alterations in the geotechnical parameters of the foundation, among others, result in non-reversible and cumulative modifications in the dam response, leading to trends in the monitoring data series. The accurate identification and definition of these trends to study their evolution are key aspects of dam safety. This manuscript proposes a methodology to identify trends in dam behavioural data series by identifying the influence of the time variable on the predictions provided by the ML models. Initially, ICE curves and SHAP values are employed to extract temporal dependence, and the ICE curves are found to be more precise and efficient in terms of computational cost. The temporal dependencies found are adjusted using a GWO algorithm to different function characteristics of irreversible processes in dams. The function that provides the best fit is selected as the most plausible. The results obtained allow us to conclude that the proposed methodology is capable of obtaining estimates of the most common trends that affect movements in concrete dams with greater precision than the statistical models most commonly used to predict the behaviour of these types of variables. These results are promising for its general application to other types of dam monitoring data series, given the versatility demonstrated for the unsupervised identification of temporal dependencies.

techniques.name: Factor Analysis
techniques.description: Factor analysis looks for a small number of hidden factors that explain why a larger set of measured variables, such as a model's input features, tend to move together. Each variable is modelled as a weighted mix of the shared factors plus a part that is unique to it, including measurement error. The weights are called loadings, and they show which variables each factor is built from; for example, several credit-history features might all load on one 'repayment behaviour' factor. Unlike principal component analysis, which summarises as much of the total variation as it can, factor analysis models only the variation that variables share. Analysts usually rotate the factors afterwards, using varimax (factors stay uncorrelated) or oblimin (factors may correlate), so that each variable loads mainly on one factor and the factors are easier to name.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team finds that forty macroeconomic and credit-bureau inputs to a default-risk model are heavily correlated. Exploratory factor analysis groups them into four factors the team can name, such as growth, inflation, household debt and credit conditions, and the model is rebuilt on the factor scores so its drivers can be explained to the risk committee in four terms instead of forty.

A flood-forecasting team with sixty correlated gauge, soil-moisture and satellite inputs runs factor analysis on the training data to find a few underlying drivers, such as rainfall intensity, catchment wetness and river level. Forecast explanations are then reported per driver, which operators can relate to what they see on the ground.

limitations.description: The standard model is linear, with each variable a weighted sum of factors plus noise. Maximum-likelihood extraction also assumes roughly normal data, so skewed, binary or strongly non-linear variables can distort the loadings. Check distributions first, or choose an extraction method that does not require normality.

Factors are statistical summaries of correlation, not discovered causes. A factor labelled 'economic confidence' is the analyst's reading of which variables load together, and a different rotation or sample may support a different label.

Sensitive to the choice of number of factors and rotation method, which have no single correct answer and can change both which variables group together and how readable the factors are. Report the choices made and check that the structure is stable.
Requires a sample that is large relative to the number of variables. With small samples the loadings are unstable and change when a few cases are added or removed.

Describes the structure of the data fed into it, not how a trained model uses that data. Factors of a model's inputs say nothing about which factors the model relies on, unless the model is also built on or analysed with the factor scores.

Overview and confirmatory and exploratory factor analysis of AI literacy scale
resources.abstract: Comprehensive concepts of AI literacy (AIL) and valid measures are essential for research (e.g., intervention studies) and practice (e.g., personnel selection/development) alike. To date, several scales have been published, sharing standard features but differing in some aspects. We first aim to briefly overview instruments identified from unsystematic literature research in February 2023. We identified four scales and one collection of items. We describe the instruments and compare them. We identified common themes and overlaps in the instruments and developmental procedure. We also found differences regarding scale development procedures and latent dimensions. Following this literature research, we came to the conclusion that the literature on AI literacy measurement was fragmented, and little effort was undertaken to integrate different AI literacy conceptualizations. The second focus of this study is to test the factorial structures of existing AIL measurement instruments and identify latent dimensions of AIL across all instruments. We used robust maximum-likelihood confirmatory factor analysis to test factorial structures in a joint survey of all AIL items in an English-speaking online sample ( N =219). We found general support for all instruments' factorial structures with minor deviations from the original factorial structures for some of the instruments. In a second analysis step, to address the issue of fragmented research on AI literacy conceptualization and measurement, we used principal axis exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation to identify latent dimensions across all items. We found four correlated latent dimensions of AIL, which were mostly interpretable as the abilities to use and interact with AI, to design/program AI (incl. in-depth technical knowledge), to perform complex cognitive operations regarding AI (e.g., ethical considerations), and a common factor for the abilities to detect AI/differentiate between AI and humans and manage persuasive influences of AI (i.e., persuasion literacy). Our findings sort the multitude of AIL instruments and reveal four latent core dimensions of AIL. Thus, they contribute importantly to the conceptual understanding of AIL that has been fragmented so far. • We give an overview of AI literacy measures. • Their factorial structures were mostly confirmed. • PA EFA identified four correlated latent dimensions across all instruments.

techniques.name: Principal Component Analysis
techniques.description: Principal component analysis (PCA) summarises a dataset that has many numeric features by finding a few new axes along which the data varies most. Each axis, called a principal component, is a weighted mix of the original features. The first axis follows the direction of greatest spread in the data, the second follows the greatest remaining spread at right angles to the first, and so on. Plotting the data on the first two or three axes gives a view of its structure, and the weights show which features move together.

example_use_cases.description: A retail analyst runs PCA on three dozen customer behaviour measures and finds that two components account for most of the variation. The weights show that one axis mixes spend and basket size and the other mixes visit frequency and recency, which gives the team a short list of dimensions to examine before building a segmentation model.

A team building a face verification system runs PCA on its training images and displays the leading components as images. If those components mainly capture lighting or background rather than face shape, the team knows the dataset's main variation reflects how the photos were taken, and can change what it collects.

A researcher auditing a word embedding takes the difference vectors for ten gendered word pairs, such as he and she, and runs PCA. The first component explains far more variance than the rest and far more than for random vectors, which suggests the embedding encodes gender mostly along one direction (Bolukbasi et al., 2016).

limitations.description: Each component mixes many original features, so it often has no clear real-world meaning, and the weights are hard to read when there are many features.
PCA captures only linear structure, so it can miss curved or clustered patterns in the data and interactions between features.

Results depend on feature scaling. PCA centres the data but does not rescale it, so a feature measured in large units can dominate the leading components. Standardise features first, or the components may reflect units and not structure.

PCA ranks directions by how much the data varies, not by how much they matter for an outcome. A high-variance component may be noise or irrelevant to a decision, and a low-variance one may carry the signal that separates classes, so leading components are not a guide to what a model needs.

Dropping components discards the variance they carry. Deciding how many to keep is a judgement call, for example a target share of variance explained, and it trades a simpler summary against lost detail.

resources.title: Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings
resources.abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. We define metrics to quantify both direct and indirect gender biases in embeddings, and develop algorithms to "debias" the embedding. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

The leading component of the portfolio's risk indicators loads on a recognisable group of related measures, so the main source of variation in the indicators can be named and discussed with the risk committee.
The training images' leading principal components have been inspected and are not dominated by capture artefacts such as lighting or sensor noise.

techniques.name: t-SNE
techniques.description: t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding) turns high-dimensional data into a two- or three-dimensional map that can be plotted and inspected. It is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method, so it can unfold curved structure that linear methods such as principal component analysis, which find only straight-line directions of greatest variation, would flatten. For each pair of points it works out how likely they are to be neighbours in the original space. It then moves the points around on the map until the same neighbour probabilities hold there as closely as possible. Because it concentrates on keeping near neighbours together, clusters of similar items usually appear as visible groups, whether the points are raw data or a model's internal representations such as embeddings.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group maps the gene-expression profiles of several thousand tumour samples with t-SNE and checks whether samples of the same clinical subtype form groups before training a subtype classifier. Subtypes that overlap on the map tell the team where the classifier is likely to confuse them.

An image-classification team maps the final hidden-layer activations of a trained network with t-SNE, colouring points by predicted class. It checks whether cars, animals and furniture fall into separate regions and which classes the network places close together, before reviewing misclassifications.

A trust-and-safety team maps the sentence embeddings used by a content-moderation model, colouring each post by the moderators' label. It checks whether flagged posts form their own group or sit among harmless posts on the same topic, and so decides whether the embedding needs retraining.

limitations.description: Results depend on random initialisation and a non-convex optimisation, so separate runs can lay clusters out differently. Fix the random seed, or start from a principal component analysis, and compare several runs before drawing conclusions.
Only local neighbourhoods are reliably preserved. Cluster sizes and the gaps between clusters carry no dependable meaning, so reading distance between groups as similarity will mislead a reviewer.

Perplexity (roughly the number of neighbours each point considers) and the number of iterations change the picture a great deal. Low settings can make random noise look like clusters, so a single plot at a single setting is weak evidence.
Standard t-SNE needs time and memory that grow with the square of the number of points, so datasets beyond roughly 10,000 points need an approximate variant or a subsample.

resources.title: Visualizing Data using t-SNE
resources.abstract:
We present a new technique called "t-SNE" that visualizes
high-dimensional data by giving each datapoint a location in a two or
three-dimensional map. The technique is a variation of Stochastic
Neighbor Embedding (Hinton and Roweis, 2002) that is much easier to optimize,
and produces significantly better visualizations by reducing the
tendency to crowd points together in the center of the map. t-SNE is
better than existing techniques at creating a single map that reveals
structure at many different scales. This is particularly important for
high-dimensional data that lie on several different, but related,
low-dimensional manifolds, such as images ofobjects from multiple
classes seen from multiple viewpoints. For visualizing the structure
of very large data sets, we show how t-SNE can use random walks on
neighborhood graphs to allow the implicit structure of all of the data
to influence the way in which a subset of the data is displayed. We
illustrate the performance of t-SNE on a wide variety of data sets and
compare it with many other non-parametric visualization techniques,
including Sammon mapping, Isomap, and Locally Linear Embedding. The
visualizations produced by t-SNE are significantly better than those
produced by the other techniques on almost all of the data sets.

The art of using t-SNE for single-cell transcriptomics
resources.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics yields ever growing data sets containing RNA expression levels for thousands of genes from up to millions of cells. Common data analysis pipelines include a dimensionality reduction step for visualising the data in two dimensions, most frequently performed using t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE). It excels at revealing local structure in high-dimensional data, but naive applications often suffer from severe shortcomings, e.g. the global structure of the data is not represented accurately. Here we describe how to circumvent such pitfalls, and develop a protocol for creating more faithful t-SNE visualisations. It includes PCA initialisation, a high learning rate, and multi-scale similarity kernels; for very large data sets, we additionally use exaggeration and downsampling-based initialisation. We use published single-cell RNA-seq data sets to demonstrate that this protocol yields superior results compared to the naive application of t-SNE.

resources.title: Automated optimized parameters for T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding improve visualization and analysis of large datasets
resources.abstract: Accurate and comprehensive extraction of information from high-dimensional single cell datasets necessitates faithful visualizations to assess biological populations. A state-of-the-art algorithm for non-linear dimension reduction, t-SNE, requires multiple heuristics and fails to produce clear representations of datasets when millions of cells are projected. We develop opt-SNE, an automated toolkit for t-SNE parameter selection that utilizes Kullback-Leibler divergence evaluation in real time to tailor the early exaggeration and overall number of gradient descent iterations in a dataset-specific manner. The precise calibration of early exaggeration together with opt-SNE adjustment of gradient descent learning rate dramatically improves computation time and enables high-quality visualization of large cytometry and transcriptomics datasets, overcoming limitations of analysis tools with hard-coded parameters that often produce poorly resolved or misleading maps of fluorescent and mass cytometry data. In summary, opt-SNE enables superior data resolution in t-SNE space and thereby more accurate data interpretation.

sample_claims.text: The image model's specified hidden-layer representations have been mapped to show local neighbourhoods and mixed-label regions for inspection.

techniques.name: UMAP
techniques.description: UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method that turns high-dimensional data into a two- or three-dimensional map for plotting. It assumes the data lie on a lower-dimensional curved surface, called a manifold, and links each point to its nearest neighbours, giving each link a strength that says how likely the two points are to be neighbours. It then arranges the points on the map so that the link strengths there match those in the original space as closely as possible. Like t-SNE, it concentrates on keeping near neighbours together, so groups of similar items appear as clusters, whether the points are raw data or a model's embeddings. Its authors argue that it keeps more of the large-scale layout than t-SNE and runs faster, but gaps between clusters and cluster sizes should not be read as exact.

example_use_cases.description: A bioinformatics team projects single-cell expression data with UMAP and checks whether cell populations annotated by hand form distinct groups before using those labels to train a classifier. Populations that merge on the map are flagged as labels the classifier may struggle to separate.

A language-technology team projects the sentence embeddings of a customer-support classifier with UMAP, colouring each message by the queue the model routes it to. It checks whether each queue is a coherent topic or a mix of unrelated ones, and decides whether to retrain the model.

A retail analytics team reduces several hundred behavioural and demographic features to two dimensions with UMAP and colours customers by the segments used in a churn model. It checks whether the segments occupy separate regions and where they overlap, so that segment boundaries are treated as soft.

limitations.description: The number of neighbours sets the scale at which structure is detected. Small values show fine detail but fragment the data and read noise as structure, and large values blur small groups, so the same dataset can tell different stories. Report the settings used.

UMAP preserves neighbourhood topology, not distances or densities. Gaps between clusters and cluster sizes should not be read as quantities, and the map's axes have no meaning, so it cannot show which features separate the groups.
It can find apparent structure in noise, especially in small or very noisy samples, where the authors warn of poor maps below about 500 points. A tidy-looking cluster is not evidence on its own.
Results vary between runs and under subsampling because neighbour search and optimisation are stochastic. Fix the random seed and check that the conclusion survives a rerun on a subsample.

It rests on a chosen distance measure and on the data forming a connected, locally smooth manifold. Where the distance suits the data badly, for example mixed numeric and categorical features, the neighbour graph and so the map may mislead.

resources.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction
resources.abstract: UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a novel manifold learning technique for dimension reduction. UMAP is constructed from a theoretical framework based in Riemannian geometry and algebraic topology. The result is a practical scalable algorithm that applies to real world data. The UMAP algorithm is competitive with t-SNE for visualization quality, and arguably preserves more of the global structure with superior run time performance. Furthermore, UMAP has no computational restrictions on embedding dimension, making it viable as a general purpose dimension reduction technique for machine learning.

resources.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
resources.abstract: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is a dimension reduction technique that can be used for visualisation similarly to t-SNE, but also for general non-linear dimension reduction. UMAP has a rigorous mathematical foundation, but is simple to use, with a scikit-learn compatible API. UMAP is among the fastest manifold learning implementations available -significantly faster than most t-SNE implementations.

Dimensionality reduction for visualizing single-cell data using UMAP
resources.abstract: Advances in single-cell technologies have enabled high-resolution dissection of tissue composition. Several tools for dimensionality reduction are available to analyze the large number of parameters generated in single-cell studies. Recently, a nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), was developed for the analysis of any type of high-dimensional data. Here we apply it to biological data, using three well-characterized mass cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. Comparing the performance of UMAP with five other tools, we find that UMAP provides the fastest run times, highest reproducibility and the most meaningful organization of cell clusters. The work highlights the use of UMAP for improved visualization and interpretation of single-cell data.

resources.title: Dimensionality reduction by UMAP to visualize physical and genetic interactions
resources.abstract: Dimensionality reduction is often used to visualize complex expression profiling data. Here, we use the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) method on published transcript profiles of 1484 single gene deletions of Saccharomyces cerevisiae . Proximity in low-dimensional UMAP space identifies groups of genes that correspond to protein complexes and pathways, and finds novel protein interactions, even within well-characterized complexes. This approach is more sensitive than previous methods and should be broadly useful as additional transcriptome datasets become available for other organisms.

sample_claims.text: Cell populations annotated by the biology team form distinct, separable groups in a UMAP projection of the expression data, and the grouping holds across three settings of the neighbour count.
The fraud model's hidden-layer representations place flagged and unflagged transactions in largely separate regions of a UMAP projection, and the pattern repeats across five random seeds.
The perception model's embeddings of pedestrian and cyclist images form separate groups in a UMAP projection, and the overlapping region has been listed for review.
Cases that the triage model assigns to different priority bands occupy separable regions in a UMAP projection of the case features, and cases lying between regions have been reviewed by a caseworker.

techniques.name: Prototype and Criticism Models
techniques.description: Prototype and criticism methods summarise a dataset with a small set of real examples. Prototypes are instances chosen to represent the bulk of the data, so that together they match its overall distribution as closely as possible. Criticisms are the instances the prototypes represent worst, which shows what the summary leaves out. In a set of customer transactions, prototypes might be the usual buying patterns and criticisms might be bulk buyers or one-off high-value customers. A reviewer can read a few dozen examples instead of the whole dataset, but the method describes the data only, so how a model performs on the unusual cases needs a separate check.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology team summarises a medical imaging dataset with prototypes and criticisms. The prototypes show the typical scans that dominate the data, and the criticisms show rare presentations the data covers thinly. The team uses the criticisms to choose cases for a separate check of how accurate the model is on rare presentations.

A credit risk team summarises its borrower records with prototypes (typical low-risk profiles) and criticisms (unusual but legitimate patterns, such as irregular self-employed income). It passes the criticism cases to a separate accuracy check, to see whether the scoring model handles them as well as typical borrowers.

An engineer preparing a visual inspection model for a production line computes prototypes and criticisms for each defect class on the model's image embeddings. The criticisms show unusual captures, such as odd lighting or partial views, which the team adds to the test set so the model is checked on them.

limitations.description: Which examples are chosen depends on the similarity measure and its settings, so different reasonable choices give different prototypes and criticisms. The original paper lists the effect of the kernel choice as future work, so there is no settled guidance.
The method needs a similarity score between every pair of examples, so memory and time grow with the square of the dataset size. Large datasets may need to be sampled before the method is run.
The user sets the number of prototypes and criticisms. Too few leaves large parts of the data unrepresented, and too many defeats the purpose of a summary short enough for a person to read.

It describes the data, not the model. Criticisms are the examples the prototypes represent worst, which is not the same as the examples the model gets wrong, so a separate evaluation is needed to learn how the model performs on them.

The original evidence that criticisms help people understand a dataset is a pilot study with four participants. Those who saw prototypes and criticisms were more accurate but slower than those who saw prototypes alone, so the benefit for a given audience is untested.

resources.title: MMD-Critic (BeenKim/MMD-Critic)
Examples are not Enough, Learn to Criticize! Criticism for Interpretability
resources.abstract: Example-based explanations are widely used in the effort to improve the interpretability of highly complex distributions. However, prototypes alone are rarely sufficient to represent the gist of the complexity. In order for users to construct better mental models and understand complex data distributions, we also need criticism to explain what are not captured by prototypes. Motivated by the Bayesian model criticism framework, we develop MMD-critic which efficiently learns prototypes and criticism, designed to aid human interpretability. A human subject pilot study shows that the MMD-critic selects prototypes and criticism that are useful to facilitate human understanding and reasoning. We also evaluate the prototypes selected by MMD-critic via a nearest prototype classifier, showing competitive performance compared to baselines.

resources.title: Prototype selection for interpretable classification
resources.abstract: Prototype methods seek a minimal subset of samples that can serve as a distillation or condensed view of a data set. As the size of modern data sets grows, being able to present a domain specialist with a short list of "representative" samples chosen from the data set is of increasing interpretative value. While much recent statistical research has been focused on producing sparse-in-the-variables methods, this paper aims at achieving sparsity in the samples. We discuss a method for selecting prototypes in the classification setting (in which the samples fall into known discrete categories). Our method of focus is derived from three basic properties that we believe a good prototype set should satisfy. This intuition is translated into a set cover optimization problem, which we solve approximately using standard approaches. While prototype selection is usually viewed as purely a means toward building an efficient classifier, in this paper we emphasize the inherent value of having a set of prototypical elements. That said, by using the nearest-neighbor rule on the set of prototypes, we can of course discuss our method as a classifier as well.

techniques.name: Influence Functions
techniques.description: Influence functions estimate which training examples most affected a model's prediction on a particular test example. For each training example, they estimate how much the model's loss on the test example would change if that example counted slightly more or slightly less, which approximates removing it and retraining without actually doing so. The estimate combines the gradient of the loss at the test and training points with the Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives, which describes the curvature of the training loss). The output ranks training examples as helpful or harmful for that prediction; because the theory assumes a smooth, convex loss, for deep networks the ranking is approximate, pointing to examples worth inspecting for mislabelled or unrepresentative cases rather than proving why the model erred. In a bias-diagnosis use, the rejections of a group already known from a separate check to be rejected more often are explained one by one, to find the training records that drive them.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital analytics team finds that its readmission model misclassifies many children. For a misclassified child, influence functions single out a handful of paediatric training records with far more influence than any others, showing that the training data holds very few children. The team collects more paediatric data before deciding whether the model can be used on that group.

An email-security team asks why its spam filter blocked a legitimate supplier invoice. It lists the training emails with the most influence on that decision, finds near-duplicate phishing messages with a similar layout, and decides whether to relabel, remove or down-weight them before retraining the filter.

A bank's model-risk team has found, from a separate check of approval rates by group, that applicants from one protected group are rejected more often. It takes a sample of that group's rejected applications and lists, for each, the training loans with the greatest influence on the rejection. It reviews whether those records are historical rejections made under discontinued underwriting rules or by branches with a known bias, and decides whether to remove or re-weight them.

limitations.description: Exact influence needs the inverse of the Hessian, which is out of reach for networks with millions of parameters. Implementations approximate it with Hessian-vector products or block-diagonal and low-rank forms, which still costs extra passes over the training data for every prediction explained and adds error. Plan to explain a sample of decisions, not all of them.

Needs the full training set, the loss function and parameters at or near a minimum of the training loss. A model delivered as an API or a finished file, or trained on data the assessor cannot see, cannot be examined. For models that are early-stopped or not trained to a minimum, the paper adds a damping term to the Hessian, one more setting that can change the ranking.

The derivation assumes a convex, twice-differentiable loss. On a non-convex CNN the paper still found a 0.86 correlation with actual retraining, but a larger study found estimates often erroneous for deeper networks and dependent on architecture, weight decay and the test point (Basu et al., 2020). Check the estimates against real retraining on a few examples before relying on them.

Losses with kinks, such as the hinge loss of a support vector machine, break the method. In the paper, influence computed on the unsmoothed hinge loss considerably overestimated the effect of removal, and a smooth approximation of the loss was needed. Check that the loss is smooth for the model in hand, or smooth it for the calculation.

resources.title: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions
resources.abstract: How can we explain the predictions of a black-box model? In this paper, we use influence functions — a classic technique from robust statistics — to trace a model's prediction through the learning algorithm and back to its training data, thereby identifying training points most responsible for a given prediction. To scale up influence functions to modern machine learning settings, we develop a simple, efficient implementation that requires only oracle access to gradients and Hessian-vector products. We show that even on non-convex and non-differentiable models where the theory breaks down, approximations to influence functions can still provide valuable information. On linear models and convolutional neural networks, we demonstrate that influence functions are useful for multiple purposes: understanding model behavior, debugging models, detecting dataset errors, and even creating visually-indistinguishable training-set attacks.

resources.title: Explaining Black Box Predictions and Unveiling Data Artifacts through Influence Functions
resources.abstract: Modern deep learning models for NLP are notoriously opaque.This has motivated the development of methods for interpreting such models, e.g., via gradient-based saliency maps or the visualization of attention weights.Such approaches aim to provide explanations for a particular model prediction by highlighting important words in the corresponding input text.While this might be useful for tasks where decisions are explicitly influenced by individual tokens in the input, we suspect that such highlighting is not always suitable for tasks where model decisions should be driven by more complex reasoning.In this work, we investigate the use of influence functions for NLP, providing an alternative approach to interpreting neural text classifiers.Influence functions explain the decisions of a model by identifying influential training examples.Despite the promise of this approach, influence functions have not yet been extensively evaluated in the context of NLP, a gap addressed by this work.We conduct a comparison between influence functions and common word-saliency methods on representative tasks.As suspected, we find that influence functions are particularly useful for natural language inference, a task in which 'saliency maps' may not provide clear interpretation.Furthermore, we develop a new quantitative measure based on influence functions that can reveal artifacts in training data.

techniques.name: Permutation Tests
techniques.description: A permutation test asks how likely an observed result would be if there were no real relationship in the data. The tester shuffles the data many times in a way that breaks the relationship under test, recalculates the metric each time, and takes the p-value as the share of shuffled results at least as extreme as the real one. Shuffling the outcome labels and retraining tests whether a classifier's accuracy beats chance, and shuffling group membership tests whether a gap between groups in the rate of decisions, such as approvals, is larger than chance would produce. A restricted variant, Ojala and Garriga's second test, shuffles each feature's values separately within each class, which keeps every feature's own spread but breaks the relationships between features, so a classifier that makes significantly fewer errors on the real data than on the shuffled copies is using those relationships. The test needs no assumption about the shape of the data's distribution, but a small p-value does not show that an effect is large, important or causal.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research group trains a classifier on 80 patients with thousands of gene-expression measurements. With so few cases, a good cross-validated accuracy could be luck, so it repeats the whole training and testing procedure on thousands of label-shuffled copies and reports the result only if it beats nearly all of them.

A council analytics team replacing a case-prioritisation model checks whether the new model's higher accuracy on the same test cases could be chance. It randomly swaps the two models' predictions case by case 10,000 times, recomputes the gap each time, and switches only if the real gap is larger than nearly all of the shuffled ones.

A bank's model-risk team sees a higher approval rate for one applicant group than another in a loan model's decisions. Before escalating, it shuffles group membership across applicants thousands of times and recomputes the gap, to test whether a gap this large could arise by chance. A significant gap prompts a fuller review but does not by itself show unlawful discrimination.

A cardiology team using a gradient-boosted model to flag high blood pressure expects height and weight to matter together, not only alone. It shuffles each feature within each outcome class 1,000 times and tests at the 5% level whether the model errs less on the real data, to decide if a simpler model treating features separately would do. A non-significant result means either the features are unrelated within classes or the model ignores the relationship.

limitations.description: Each permutation needs the metric recalculated, and a model may need retraining every time, so thousands of permutations of a large model can be expensive. Stricter thresholds need more permutations, because the smallest possible p-value is 1 divided by the number of permutations plus one, and repeated runs can disagree near the threshold.

Assumes exchangeability of observations under the null hypothesis, which may be violated in time series or hierarchical data structures, where simple shuffling gives p-values that are too small or too large.

A significant result shows that the data are unlikely under the stated null, such as 'features and labels are independent'. It does not show that the effect is large, important or causal, and shuffling cannot rule out a confounder or an artefact of how the data were collected.

Testing many features or groups at once produces some false positives by chance, so the p-values need correcting, for example with a false discovery rate procedure. Without that, a feature-by-feature test over many features will flag some that are only noise.

What is shuffled defines the question answered. Shuffling labels tests whether features and labels are related at all, while shuffling features within classes tests whether a classifier uses dependencies between features. The wrong scheme answers a different question from the one the assurance claim needs.

Permutation Tests for Studying Classifier Performance
resources.abstract: We explore the framework of permutation-based p-values for assessing the behavior of the classification error. In this paper we study two simple permutation tests. The first test estimates the null distribution by permuting the labels in the data; this has been used extensively in classification problems in computational biology. The second test produces permutations of the features within classes, inspired by restricted randomization techniques traditionally used in statistics. We study the properties of these tests and present an extensive empirical evaluation on real and synthetic data. Our analysis shows that studying the classification error via permutation tests is effective; in particular, the restricted permutation test clearly reveals whether the classifier exploits the interdependency between the features in the data.

resources.title: Nonparametric permutation tests for functional neuroimaging: A primer with examples
resources.abstract: Requiring only minimal assumptions for validity, nonparametric permutation testing provides a flexible and intuitive methodology for the statistical analysis of data from functional neuroimaging experiments, at some computational expense. Introduced into the functional neuroimaging literature by Holmes et al. ([ 1996 ]: J Cereb Blood Flow Metab 16:7–22), the permutation approach readily accounts for the multiple comparisons problem implicit in the standard voxel‐by‐voxel hypothesis testing framework. When the appropriate assumptions hold, the nonparametric permutation approach gives results similar to those obtained from a comparable Statistical Parametric Mapping approach using a general linear model with multiple comparisons corrections derived from random field theory. For analyses with low degrees of freedom, such as single subject PET/SPECT experiments or multi‐subject PET/SPECT or f MRI designs assessed for population effects, the nonparametric approach employing a locally pooled (smoothed) variance estimate can outperform the comparable Statistical Parametric Mapping approach. Thus, these nonparametric techniques can be used to verify the validity of less computationally expensive parametric approaches. Although the theory and relative advantages of permutation approaches have been discussed by various authors, there has been no accessible explication of the method, and no freely distributed software implementing it. Consequently, there have been few practical applications of the technique. This article, and the accompanying MATLAB software, attempts to address these issues. The standard nonparametric randomization and permutation testing ideas are developed at an accessible level, using practical examples from functional neuroimaging, and the extensions for multiple comparisons described. Three worked examples from PET and f MRI are presented, with discussion, and comparisons with standard parametric approaches made where appropriate. Practical considerations are given throughout, and relevant statistical concepts are expounded in appendices.

techniques.name: Algorithm Review Boards
techniques.description: An algorithm review board, also called an AI ethics board or AI review board, is a standing group from different disciplines that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects before they proceed. It differs from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because it also weighs harms to the people a system will affect and to society. Many boards first sort projects by risk, and for higher-risk work the project team submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, which members with technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds question and iterate on with the team. Where it has the power to decide, the board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects; where it only advises, it recommends one of these. It keeps a dated record of its decision, reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built, and some organisations share that record with an oversight body or publish it.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group's algorithm review board examines a sepsis early-warning model before a ward pilot. It approves the pilot on condition of a monitoring plan for alert rates and missed cases, names who may switch the model off, and sets a re-review once six months of local performance data are in, before any wider roll-out.

A bank's board reviews a proposed credit-limit model before launch. It asks the team for its disparate-impact analysis by protected group and for evidence that applicants can contest a decision, and withholds approval until both are supplied, so the decision to deploy rests with a body outside the development team.

A university AI research programme releases grant funding only after each project has passed an ethics and society review, in which researchers state the risks their work poses to society and to particular groups, commit to mitigations, and revise them with an interdisciplinary faculty panel.

A government department publishes the board's decision record for a benefits-triage tool, giving the reasons for approval, the conditions attached and the re-review date, so that its oversight committee and the public can see what was examined, by whom and when, and check later that the conditions were met.

limitations.description: Review adds time and cost to every project that goes through it, and organisations under commercial pressure may route work around the board or narrow its remit, so the board's coverage, not just its existence, needs to be shown.

Its judgements are only as good as its membership. A board without the relevant technical, domain or community expertise will miss harms that fall outside what its members know, and a board drawn mainly from inside the team's own reporting line is open to group-think.

Independence is hard to keep inside an organisation. Practitioners report tension between profit and the cost of responsible-AI review, and a board can come under pressure to approve projects that leadership has already committed to, which weakens it most where review matters most.

Without authority to stop or delay a project, and a way to check that its conditions are met, a board's recommendations can be ignored. Evidence from a board is strong only when its decision record shows what it could block and what happened to its conditions.

There is no agreed measure of whether a board works, and review can become box-ticking. A record that a project was reviewed shows that a process ran, not that the review was substantive or that its concerns were addressed.

resources.title: How to design an AI ethics board
resources.abstract: The development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems poses significant risks to society. To reduce these risks to an acceptable level, AI companies need an effective risk management process and sound risk governance. In this paper, we explore a particular way in which AI companies can improve their risk governance: by setting up an AI ethics board. We identify five key design choices: (1) What responsibilities should the board have? (2) What should its legal structure be? (3) Who should sit on the board? (4) How should it make decisions? (5) And what resources does it need? We break each of these questions down into more specific sub-questions, list options, and discuss how different design choices affect the board’s ability to reduce societal risks from AI. Several failures have shown that designing an AI ethics board can be challenging. This paper provides a toolbox that can help AI companies to overcome these challenges.

resources.title: Designing Artificial Intelligence Review Boards: Creating Risk Metrics for Review of AI
resources.abstract: Discussions of the need for a review committee dedicated to ethical oversight of artificial intelligence (AI) research have not yet advanced to organization design discussions. What are the essential components for an AI research review board? Based upon precedent for composition and conduct of high-technology review boards, one essential component is a risk-adjusted review mechanism that assists review boards in the categorization of research needing review. In this paper, risk assessment tools are developed based upon lessons learned from other review boards, such as Institutional Biosafety Committees.

resources.title: Ethics and society review: Ethics reflection as a precondition to research funding
resources.abstract: Researchers in areas as diverse as computer science and political science must increasingly navigate the possible risks of their research to society. However, the history of medical experiments on vulnerable individuals influenced many research ethics reviews to focus exclusively on risks to human subjects rather than risks to human society. We describe an Ethics and Society Review board (ESR), which fills this moral gap by facilitating ethical and societal reflection as a requirement to access grant funding: Researchers cannot receive grant funding from participating programs until the researchers complete the ESR process for their proposal. Researchers author an initial statement describing their proposed research’s risks to society, subgroups within society, and globally and commit to mitigation strategies for these risks. An interdisciplinary faculty panel iterates with the researchers to refine these risks and mitigation strategies. We describe a mixed-method evaluation of the ESR over 1 y, in partnership with an artificial intelligence grant program run by Stanford HAI. Surveys and interviews of researchers who interacted with the ESR found 100% (95% CI: 87 to 100%) were willing to continue submitting future projects to the ESR, and 58% (95% CI: 37 to 77%) felt that it had influenced the design of their research project. The ESR panel most commonly identified issues of harms to minority groups, inclusion of diverse stakeholders in the research plan, dual use, and representation in datasets. These principles, paired with possible mitigation strategies, offer scaffolding for future research designs.

resources.title: ESR Process & Toolkit — Stanford Ethics & Society Review
resources.abstract: The Ethics and Society Review is improving ethical reflection in research by bringing together a panel of ethics experts to help researchers identify and mitigate negative ethical or societal aspects of their research and elevate the positive.

resources.title: Investigating Algorithm Review Boards for Organizational Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance
resources.abstract: Organizations are increasingly developing and utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Responsible AI (RAI) governance approaches including algorithm review board (ARBs) have emerged as important mechanisms to address potential AI risks and harms. We interviewed 17 technical contributors at a variety of organizations about their experiences with internal RAI governance. We summarized the first detailed findings on ARBs in practice, including their membership, scope, and measures of success. We confirmed known ARBs in finance sectors and revealed extensive use of ARBs in health sectors. Our findings suggest that Institutional Review Boards alone are insufficient for algorithm governance and that ARBs are used in tandem with other RAI approaches. Integration with existing processes and leadership buy-in were considered critical to the success of internal RAI governance. Financial tensions between profit and the cost of RAI were a major concern for many participants. Future work should explore measurements of success for ARBs and expand analysis of ARBs to other industries leading in AI implementation.

resources.title: A framework for the oversight and local deployment of safe and high-quality prediction models
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence/machine learning models are being rapidly developed and used in clinical practice. However, many models are deployed without a clear understanding of clinical or operational impact and frequently lack monitoring plans that can detect potential safety signals. There is a lack of consensus in establishing governance to deploy, pilot, and monitor algorithms within operational healthcare delivery workflows. Here, we describe a governance framework that combines current regulatory best practices and lifecycle management of predictive models being used for clinical care. Since January 2021, we have successfully added models to our governance portfolio and are currently managing 52 models.

techniques.name: Red Teaming
techniques.description: Red teaming is a structured exercise in which a team deliberately tries to make an AI system fail, so that weaknesses are found before real users or attackers find them. The organisers set the scope and the harms of concern, recruit people with a mix of skills (for example security testers, domain specialists and members of affected groups), and give them a way to log each attempt and judge whether it worked. Participants try manipulative prompts, awkward edge cases and requests designed to draw out harmful, insecure or discriminatory responses, combining many approaches where a test for one known weakness, such as prompt injection, covers only one. The result is a record of the failures found and how easily each was provoked, which is not a pass or fail verdict. It feeds a risk register (the list of known risks and who owns them) and fixes, and the exercise is repeated when the system changes.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital convenes clinicians, medical students and engineers to stress-test a language model that drafts clinical notes, using real patient cases. Each response that could harm a patient, such as a wrong dosage, is logged and sent to the clinical safety officer to decide on fixes and on how staff may use the tool.

Before launch, a bank's security team and outside testers spend two weeks trying to make its customer-service assistant leak client data or obey instructions hidden in uploaded documents. Each successful attack is written up with the steps to reproduce it and ranked by how easily it was exploited, so engineers can fix the worst first.

A local authority asks advice charities and its own caseworkers to probe a chatbot that explains benefit entitlements. They look for answers that differ or discourage claims depending on a person's nationality, disability or first language, and record each case with the prompt that provoked it, for the authority to fix or justify.

An insurer's AI governance committee requires a red-team report before any customer-facing model goes live. Findings are entered in the risk register with an owner and a due date, and the committee signs off only when each high-severity item is fixed or formally accepted.

limitations.description: Needs people who understand both the system and how attackers work, and some harms need domain specialists to judge, for example whether chemical instructions are accurate. Exercises are therefore costly and hard to scale across many systems.

Finds only what the team thinks to try. In Anthropic's original exercise with 324 crowd workers, no attacks targeted code generation although the models had been trained partly on code, so coverage depends on who is recruited and how they are briefed.

Results describe one model version, configuration and set of safeguards at one moment. After an update or a prompt change, fixed failures can return and new ones appear, so the exercise has to be repeated, which adds cost each time.

Tester-written attacks may differ from real misuse, and there is no agreed measure of success. In Anthropic's study, participants' own ratings and an automated harm score correlated only imperfectly, and a minority of participants produced most attacks, so exercises are hard to compare.

A report with few findings can be read as proof of safety when it shows only that this team did not find a failure in the time available. Reports should state scope, effort and what was not tried, or they invite false confidence.

resources.title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned
resources.abstract: We describe our early efforts to red team language models in order to simultaneously discover, measure, and attempt to reduce their potentially harmful outputs. We make three main contributions. First, we investigate scaling behaviors for red teaming across 3 model sizes (2.7B, 13B, and 52B parameters) and 4 model types: a plain language model (LM); an LM prompted to be helpful, honest, and harmless; an LM with rejection sampling; and a model trained to be helpful and harmless using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). We find that the RLHF models are increasingly difficult to red team as they scale, and we find a flat trend with scale for the other model types. Second, we release our dataset of 38,961 red team attacks for others to analyze and learn from. We provide our own analysis of the data and find a variety of harmful outputs, which range from offensive language to more subtly harmful non-violent unethical outputs. Third, we exhaustively describe our instructions, processes, statistical methodologies, and uncertainty about red teaming. We hope that this transparency accelerates our ability to work together as a community in order to develop shared norms, practices, and technical standards for how to red team language models.

resources.title: Red Teaming LLM Applications - DeepLearning.AI
Red teaming ChatGPT in medicine to yield real-world insights on model behavior
resources.abstract: Red teaming, the practice of adversarially exposing unexpected or undesired model behaviors, is critical towards improving equity and accuracy of large language models, but non-model creator-affiliated red teaming is scant in healthcare. We convened teams of clinicians, medical and engineering students, and technical professionals (80 participants total) to stress-test models with real-world clinical cases and categorize inappropriate responses along axes of safety, privacy, hallucinations/accuracy, and bias. Six medically-trained reviewers re-analyzed prompt-response pairs and added qualitative annotations. Of 376 unique prompts (1504 responses), 20.1% were inappropriate (GPT-3.5: 25.8%; GPT-4.0: 16%; GPT-4.0 with Internet: 17.8%). Subsequently, we show the utility of our benchmark by testing GPT-4o, a model released after our event (20.4% inappropriate). 21.5% of responses appropriate with GPT-3.5 were inappropriate in updated models. We share insights for constructing red teaming prompts, and present our benchmark for iterative model assessments.

sample_claims.text: A red-team exercise with clinicians and engineers tested the clinical-notes assistant against the hazards in its safety case, and every high-severity failure it found has a recorded fix or an accepted-risk decision.
The customer-service assistant was red-teamed for prompt injection and extraction of client data before launch, and each successful attack was fixed and re-tested.
A red-team exercise that included people from the affected groups probed the benefits assistant for discriminatory answers, and every case found has been triaged and fixed or formally accepted.

techniques.name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
techniques.description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards hold an AI system's output at a checkpoint until a trained person has reviewed it. Designers set the rules that send a case to review, such as low model confidence (the system's own estimate of how likely it is to be right), a high-stakes outcome or a request to appeal. Some schemes also review a random sample of routine cases to audit the rest. The reviewer approves, changes or rejects the output, and the record of each review shows how often people overrode the system. Review protects only where reviewers keep using independent judgement, so the design also has to guard against over-trust and fatigue.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing mandatory human physician review for any medical AI diagnostic recommendation before treatment decisions are made, especially for complex cases or when the system confidence is below established thresholds, ensuring patient safety through expert oversight.

Requiring human review of automated loan approval decisions when applicants request explanations or appeal rejections, allowing human underwriters to provide clear reasoning and ensure customers understand the decision-making process behind their application outcomes.

A recruitment agency requires a named recruiter to confirm or reverse every automated rejection before it is sent, and logs the decision and the reason. The agency's governance board reviews the override rate each quarter to see whether the screening tool and its reviewers are working as intended.

limitations.description: Review capacity sets a ceiling. As volume rises, cases queue, decisions are delayed and time-sensitive uses become impractical, so the escalation rules must be tuned to what the available trained reviewers can handle.
Reviewers tire and drift. Attention and consistency fall over a long shift or a run of similar cases, so two reviewers, or one reviewer at different times, may decide the same case differently.

Automation bias. People tend to accept a system's recommendation, particularly under time pressure, so review can become a rubber stamp. A very high approval rate with almost no overrides may signal this rather than a good system.

The escalation rules decide what a human ever sees. A confidently wrong output passes without review when only low-confidence cases are escalated, so reviewing a random sample of routine cases is needed to find these errors.

Human review does not reliably improve decisions. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments found human-AI combinations performed worse on average than the better of human or AI alone, with losses in decision-making tasks. The effect of a checkpoint should be tested, not assumed.

resources.title: Improving the Applicability of AI for Psychiatric Applications through Human-in-the-loop Methodologies
resources.abstract: Objectives Machine learning (ML) and natural language processing have great potential to improve efficiency and accuracy in diagnosis, treatment recommendations, predictive interventions, and scarce resource allocation within psychiatry. Researchers often conceptualize such an approach as operating in isolation without much need for human involvement, yet it remains crucial to harness human-in-the-loop practices when developing and implementing such techniques as their absence may be catastrophic. We advocate for building ML-based technologies that collaborate with experts within psychiatry in all stages of implementation and use to increase model performance while simultaneously increasing the practicality, robustness, and reliability of the process. Methods We showcase pitfalls of the traditional ML framework and explain how it can be improved with human-in-the-loop techniques. Specifically, we applied active learning strategies to the automatic scoring of a story recall task and compared the results to a traditional approach. Results Human-in-the-loop methodologies supplied a greater understanding of where the model was least confident or had knowledge gaps during training. As compared to the traditional framework, less than half of the training data were needed to reach a given accuracy. Conclusions Human-in-the-loop ML is an approach to data collection and model creation that harnesses active learning to select the most critical data needed to increase a model’s accuracy and generalizability more efficiently than classic random sampling would otherwise allow. Such techniques may additionally operate as safeguards from spurious predictions and can aid in decreasing disparities that artificial intelligence systems otherwise propagate.

resources.title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
resources.abstract: Technical developments in computer hardware and software now make it possible to introduce automation into virtually all aspects of human-machine systems. Given these technical capabilities, which system functions should be automated and to what extent? We outline a model for types and levels of automation that provides a framework and an objective basis for making such choices. Appropriate selection is important because automation does not merely supplant but changes human activity and can impose new coordination demands on the human operator. We propose that automation can be applied to four broad classes of functions: 1) information acquisition; 2) information analysis; 3) decision and action selection; and 4) action implementation. Within each of these types, automation can be applied across a continuum of levels from low to high, i.e., from fully manual to fully automatic. A particular system can involve automation of all four types at different levels. The human performance consequences of particular types and levels of automation constitute primary evaluative criteria for automation design using our model. Secondary evaluative criteria include automation reliability and the costs of decision/action consequences, among others. Examples of recommended types and levels of automation are provided to illustrate the application of the model to automation design.
